slice: AI writes prescriptions, bonds sell off, and dinosaurs still fetch millions.

stories.title: AI can now prescribe acne drugs in Utah
points: From Monday, Nolla Health’s app can send acne prescriptions straight to pharmacies in Utah, the first time a state has let AI stand in for the doctor, under a ‘narrow exception’ from Utah’s Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy.
Patients scan their face and enter their medical history; the AI scores acne severity and picks from eight approved topical treatments, with no pills or hormone therapies.

Oversight tapers: a physician checks the first 100 patients before anything is sent, the next 400 weekly after the fact, and then at least 10% of prescriptions each month. The pilot runs a year, renewable for two more.
stories.why: A tightly fenced test of whether software can do a doctor’s routine job.
stories.other: Scripts still carry a clinician’s name and doctors review a share of them. The AMA’s John Whyte doubts AI can meet the standard humans are held to. A safe shortcut, or a precedent for riskier drugs?

stories.title: Japan Inc sours on China; can India gain?
points: Japanese firms with a presence in China fell to 10,118 in June, the lowest since the survey began in 2010: down 22% in two years and almost 30% from the 2012 peak of 14,394.
Reasons cited include China’s property slump, rare-earth export curbs, overcapacity, state-backed rivals, worsening relations and detentions of Japanese nationals.
Japanese money is moving into India’s finance, not just factories: SMBC bought 20% of YES Bank (~$1.6bn), MUFG 20% of Shriram Finance (~$4.45bn), and Mizuho’s securities arm a majority of Avendus.
stories.why: Japan is buying into India’s banks, not just building factories.
stories.other: China is too big to abandon, and the US, Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand compete for the same capital. Skill shortages and reliance on Chinese inputs could cap India’s gains.

stories.title: Cognizant targets mid-sized firms as AI squeezes big deals
points: Cognizant launched Cognizant Activate on Monday, a unit for companies with $1–5 billion in revenue, as AI puts pressure on the big outsourcing contracts the industry was built on.
It is the third big IT firm in six months to do this, after Accenture Edge ($300M–$3B clients) and HCLTech Pulse ($500M–$5B), and it puts Cognizant up against Coforge, Mphasis and Persistent.
It will sell pre-configured bundles in data and AI, cybersecurity, cloud and managed services, starting with financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, retail and consumer goods.
stories.why: Mid-tier IT firms now face the giants on their home turf.
stories.other: Mid-sized clients rarely award the $500 million multi-year deals tier-1 firms grew on, though analysts say there are thousands more of them and margins can be better. Can giants move small and fast?

stories.title: NPS Swasthya: a health savings fund plus top-up cover
points: The pension regulator PFRDA launched NPS Swasthya on 1 October: a healthcare investment account bundled with a mandatory super top-up group health policy.
Cover can be bought from 18 to 70 and renewed to 85, with no medical tests; a ₹30 lakh cover with a ₹3 lakh deductible costs ₹1,732 a year at 18–40 and ₹4,953 at 61–70.
Joining needs ₹1,000, a ₹200 yearly administrator fee and the first premium; the corpus can pay the deductible or network outpatient bills, but withdrawals are capped at 25% of contributions.
stories.why: Entry up to 70 without medical tests could help older buyers who struggle to get cover.
stories.other: Pre-existing diseases wait a year, about 15 serious illnesses may be excluded or cost extra, and like-for-like price comparisons are hard. The real test is how claims are handled.

stories.title: Manu Joseph: the mystery behind Tata’s boardroom ‘coup’
points: On 17 September every Tata Sons director except Noel Tata asked N. Chandrasekaran to stay on, after he had decided to leave when his term ends in February 2027.
Joseph says Noel Tata, chairman of the Trusts that own 66% of Tata Sons, has been isolated, the Trusts are divided, and there are whispers of political influence.
On listing, he argues the Trusts wouldn’t lose control if a quarter of Tata Sons floated, yet Noel Tata opposes it; the RBI wants it listed.
stories.why: Who steers India’s largest business group is now openly contested.
stories.other: The political angle rests on whispers and perception, not proof; both sides claim principle, and with 66% the Trusts’ grip can’t easily shift.

stories.title: Zimbabwe in talks to use India’s UPI tech
points: Zimbabwe is negotiating with NPCI International Payments, the overseas arm of the body that runs UPI, to use its technology as shared rails linking banks, mobile-money operators and fintechs in real time.
Central bank governor John Mushayavanhu says talks could conclude by 31 October; that is a deadline for the talks, not a launch date.
It follows NPCI International’s May 2024 deal to help Namibia build a UPI-like instant-payment system, and fits Zimbabwe’s own March push for QR codes that work across providers.
stories.why: India is exporting the payment rails, not just letting tourists pay abroad.
stories.other: Savings, fees, budget and a timetable are all undisclosed, and prices will depend on how banks and payment firms join in. Does better plumbing cut costs on its own?

stories.title: A global bond rout: why it reaches your EMI
points: The US 10-year yield closed at 5.29% on 30 September, the highest since 2002; Britain’s 30-year topped 6% for the first time since 1998, and France’s 10-year hit a near 25-year high.
Three causes at once: costly oil reviving inflation fears, the US Fed raising rates again on 16 September, and governments borrowing more than lenders like.
India’s 10-year is about 7.2%, near a two-year high; a one-point rise on a ₹50 lakh, 20-year home loan adds about ₹3,100 a month.
stories.why: Government yields set the floor for every loan, so borrowing costs rise without any central bank acting.
stories.other: Savers get better rates on new deposits and bonds, and emerging markets, India included, have held up better so far. A crisis, or a reset to normal rates?

stories.title: Investors look for shelter from AI concentration risk
points: More than two-thirds of the Russell 1000 is linked to AI, per Citigroup research, and Big Tech hyperscalers and AI beneficiaries are about 16% of the US high-grade bond market, its biggest group.
Fund managers at Amundi, BlackRock and Franklin Templeton say clients want returns that don’t move with AI: global macro and long-short hedge funds, systematic strategies, mining and renewables.

Amundi’s Vincent Mortier says clients are looking more at emerging markets, including local stocks and bonds in India, China and Latin America; a turn in AI is ‘not imminent’, he says, ‘but I think it will come’.
numbers: large US firms tied to AI
AI build-out by a few firms
stories.why: When one theme dominates both US stocks and bonds, spreading risk gets hard.
stories.other: The same managers say no sell-off is imminent, and the right hedge funds are hard to find and often closed. Prudence, or trying to time the market?

stories.title: A rare Nanotyrannus heads to auction as the fossil boom roars on
points: Sotheby’s will sell ‘Jodi’, a Nanotyrannus found in Montana in 2019, in New York at the end of October, estimating $6–9 million; it is one of three specimens known to science.
It follows a record $50.1 million for the T. rex ‘Gus’ this year, after a 10-minute bidding battle, and Ken Griffin’s $44.6 million Stegosaurus in 2024.
A paper last year by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli settled an 80-year debate: Nanotyrannus was its own genus, not a young T. rex. Jodi is the first to sell since.
stories.why: Fossils have become a trophy asset for the very rich.
stories.other: Griffin’s Stegosaurus is on museum display, but where ‘Gus’ went isn’t public. Should rare finds that settle science debates go to private buyers?

stories.title: ‘FROGS’: France’s slow-burn debt crisis
points: Columnist Lionel Laurent says France’s bond risk premium is at a decade-plus high, with a deficit above 5% of GDP, debt near 120% and the gap over German bonds at new highs.
FROGS, coined by research firm Rexecode, stands for French Oversized Government and Social Security; he expects a slow squeeze rather than a sudden, Truss-style shock.
Debt sharing with northern Europe is off the table, and any ECB rescue risks a populist backlash, with next year’s presidential election looming.
stories.why: Bond markets, not voters, may now set France’s budget.
stories.other: He concedes France is no Greece: its economy is large and diversified and its banks well capitalised, ‘too big to bail’, as one economist puts it. Squeeze, or scare?

stories.title: Who really runs Jane Street?
points: Wall Street’s biggest trading house overtook JPMorgan last year, with almost $40 billion of trading revenue, yet has no named CEO and, on purpose, no partners list.
Regulatory records show a management committee that meets monthly and decides on risk across the firm; a few dozen people, many of them company lifers, steer it.
Co-founder Rob Granieri, the last of the four founders still there, has had no official title or headshot in the staff directory.
stories.why: If you own an ETF, it was likely traded by a firm few can map.
stories.other: The firm says a conventional org chart misses leaders spread across a flat, collaborative structure. Is opacity a risk, or its edge?
